project.title: ShopFlow: E-commerce Backend with Idempotent Checkout, Payments and AI Search
project.tagline: Build an online-shop backend that never oversells, never charges twice and never loses a payment, with AI as your pair programmer
project.description: Over nine phases you build ShopFlow like a professional team: requirements and threats, design with ADRs, a test-first implementation of a product catalog with full-text search, a server-side cart with coupons, money as integer paise, checkout with an Idempotency-Key and a guarded stock decrement that cannot oversell, orders with a state machine, HMAC-signed and de-duplicated payment webhooks, a transactional outbox, AI search assist and product description drafts with offline fallbacks, CI/CD with GitHub Actions, Docker, optional free-tier deployment, observability, a payment-window migration and a retrospective. Pick Java, Python or TypeScript; the spec, database and tests are shared. Everything runs on your laptop, and the AI features work offline.

One of: Java, Python or TypeScript fundamentals
REST APIs and HTTP status codes

outcomes: Turn a shop brief into testable requirements, user stories and a threat list (forged webhooks, double checkout, overselling, price tampering)
Design a REST API contract-first (OpenAPI) with a PostgreSQL schema, an order state machine and ADRs
Handle money correctly: integer paise end to end, exact coupon maths, database CHECK constraints
Prevent overselling with a guarded stock decrement and prove it with parallel checkout tests
Make checkout idempotent with an Idempotency-Key and payment webhooks safe with HMAC signatures and event de-duplication
Never lose an event between the database and a broker with a transactional outbox
Add AI search assist and description drafts whose output is validated and that fall back offline
Build CI/CD with GitHub Actions: matrix, caching, reusable workflows, service containers, GHCR
Add request IDs, JSON logs, metrics, a circuit breaker and an expand-only migration after a game day and a blameless post-mortem
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every output
project.ai_feature: AI search assist (natural language to validated catalog filters) and product description drafts for the owner: offline rules/template by default, optional Ollama or a free Gemini/Groq key; checkout never depends on the AI
project.portfolio_blurb: Built ShopFlow, an e-commerce REST API: money as integer paise, a guarded stock decrement proven by parallel checkout tests (no overselling), idempotent checkout with Idempotency-Key, HMAC-signed and de-duplicated payment webhooks, a transactional outbox, optimistic locking, PostgreSQL full-text search with AI search assist and offline fallback, >=85 % test coverage, GitHub Actions CI/CD to GHCR, Docker, JSON logs, metrics, a circuit breaker added after a game day and an expand-only payment-window migration.

phases.title: Setup and orientation
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup and orientation
phases.why_md:
Every professional project starts with a working local environment and a clean Git workflow. Teams
lose days to "works on my machine". In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, run the
starter, meet the test suite that will guide you, open your first pull request and start your
`AI_LOG.md`. That is the evidence a reviewer looks for first: a repo that builds from a clean checkout
with one command.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (Java, Python or TypeScript) and install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux.
Start PostgreSQL with Docker Compose and run the starter so `GET /health` returns `UP`.
Run lint and tests locally and see which tests are *pending* and why.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/ecommerce-backend` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**.
   The `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/ecommerce-backend.git
   cd ecommerce-backend
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/ecommerce-backend.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # you should see phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/ecommerce-backend`), not under `/mnt/c`. File watching and Docker volumes are 5–10× faster there.

steps.title: Install Docker and the tools for ONE track
steps.content_md:
* **All tracks:** Git, Docker (Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS with the WSL2 backend; Docker Engine +
  compose plugin on Linux), `make` and `curl`.
* Then run the doctor script. It tells you exactly what is missing:
  ```bash
  scripts/doctor.sh
  ```

<!-- track:java -->
**Java track:** JDK 21 (Temurin) and Maven 3.9+. The easiest way on Linux/macOS/WSL is SDKMAN:
```bash
curl -s https://get.sdkman.io | bash   # then open a new terminal
sdk install java 21-tem && sdk install maven
java -version && mvn -v
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
**Python track:** Python 3.11+ with `venv` (Ubuntu/WSL: `sudo apt install python3 python3-venv`;
macOS: `brew install python@3.12`).
```bash
python3 --version
cd tracks/python && make install     # creates .venv and installs pinned dependencies
```
<!-- /track -->

```bash
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.1/install.sh | bash   # new terminal
```

steps.title: Start the database
steps.content_md:
```bash
docker compose up -d postgres
docker compose ps          # postgres should be "healthy"
```
The first start also creates a second database, `shopflow_test`, that the integration tests use
(`spec/db/init/01-create-test-db.sql`), so tests can never wipe your dev data. Port 5432 already taken
(another Postgres)? Set `POSTGRES_PORT=55432` in `.env` and use that port in `DATABASE_URL`.

steps.content_md:
<!-- track:java -->
```bash

make run                   # mvn spring-boot:run, listens on :8080
```

<!-- track:typescript -->
```bash

make run                   # tsx watch src/index.ts, listens on :8080
```

In another terminal:
```bash
curl -s localhost:8080/health
# {"status":"UP","checks":{"database":"UP"}}
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
# {"type":"https://shopflow.example/problems/internal-error","title":"Internal server error","status":500}
```
The endpoints already exist, but they answer `500` because the business logic is a `TODO`: that is
Phase 3. Notice that even the crash is a clean `application/problem+json` body with no stack trace:
error handling is part of the starter. Stop the database (`docker compose stop postgres`) and call
`/health` again: it answers `503` with `"database":"DOWN"`. Start it again with `docker compose start postgres`.

(`admin@shopflow.local`). They are fine on your laptop and wrong anywhere else; Phase 6 shows how a
deployment sets its own. The log also shows `TODO(phase-3 M2): ensure_admin - starting without an
admin`: creating that admin is one of your first Phase 3 tasks.

steps.title: Run the checks and meet the pending tests
steps.content_md:
```bash
make lint test
```
You will see **a few passing tests** (`/health`, and in Java the `DATABASE_URL` parser) and well over a
hundred **skipped** ones. They are *pending*: the complete test suite for ShopFlow is already written and
switched off in one file per track:

| Track | Pending list |
|---|---|
| Java | `tracks/java/src/test/java/org/aicancode/shopflow/support/Pending.java` |
| Python | `tracks/python/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| TypeScript | `tracks/typescript/test/pending.ts` (`PENDING`) |

Open the list now. Each entry names a milestone ("Phase 3 M4 - cart endpoints"). In Phase 3 you delete
one entry at a time, watch the tests go red, and make them green.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant helped you install the toolchain and
   how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my
   workflows, go ahead and enable them"**. The CI workflow runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks.
   Wait for green, fill in the PR template and merge.

ai_prompts.title: Fix my toolchain install
ai_prompts.prompt:
I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a <Java 21 + Maven |
Python 3.12 | Node 22> project with Docker Compose. Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh:
<paste output>. Give me the exact commands to install what is missing, explain each one in one line,
and tell me how to verify each install.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: running each verification command it gives you, re-running `scripts/doctor.sh` until every line is green, and checking any download URL against the official site (adoptium.net, python.org, nodejs.org, docker.com). Never pipe an unknown URL into `bash`.

ai_prompts.title: Explain the starter
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is the file tree of a starter project and the file <tracks/<track>/…/main entry file>:
<paste>. Explain in plain English what happens from "make run" until GET /health returns, which
files are involved, where environment variables are read, and where an unexpected exception is turned
into an HTTP 500 response. Do not suggest code changes.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: finding each file and function it names (an assistant may invent ones that do not exist), then changing `PORT=8081 make run` to confirm the app really listens on the new port.

ai_prompts.title: What will I build?
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is an OpenAPI 3.1 contract: <paste spec/openapi.yaml>. Summarise in 10 bullet points what this
API does, which endpoints need authentication, which need a specific role, and which three endpoints
you expect to be the hardest to get right. Quote the path for every claim.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every quoted path and `security`/role note against the file. Mark anything it got wrong; you will meet the same contract in Phases 2 and 3.

deliverables.text: Your fork contains the `solution` branch and the `phase-*` tags (`git tag -l` shows them).
`docker compose up -d postgres` works; `GET /health` returns `UP` from your track.
`make lint test` passes locally (a few passed, the rest skipped).
A merged PR with a green CI run.
`AI_LOG.md` has its first entry.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise Docker Compose cannot find the database
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: On Windows, where should the repository live?
options: Inside the WSL2 Linux file system, e.g. `~/code/ecommerce-backend`
On a network drive so Docker can share it
quiz.explanation: Cross-file-system access from WSL to `/mnt/c` is slow and breaks file watching. Keep code in the Linux file system and open it with VS Code's WSL extension.

quiz.q: Why do integration tests use a separate `shopflow_test` database?
options: PostgreSQL allows only one connection per database
The tests empty the tables before each test, which must never touch your dev data
quiz.explanation: Integration tests truncate tables to start from a known state. A separate database (created by `spec/db/init`) makes that safe on your laptop.

quiz.q: Why are most tests skipped in the starter?
options: CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you will implement in Phases 3–4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (a test-first workflow). Deleting a line from the pending list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go into an AI prompt?
options: A stack trace from your own code
Your `.env` file with the JWT secret and API keys
quiz.explanation: Secrets and personal data never go into prompts. Anyone with the JWT secret can mint an ADMIN token for your API. Redact before you paste.

quiz.q: The starter answers `500` for `POST /api/v1/auth/register`. Why is the body still JSON without a stack trace?
options: The framework hides errors in production mode automatically
The starter already maps unexpected exceptions to a generic `problem+json` response and logs the details server-side
The endpoint is not implemented in the router
quiz.explanation: Leaking stack traces tells attackers your stack and file layout. Clients get a generic problem body; the details go to the server log.

phases.title: Requirements, threats and user stories
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Requirements, threats and user stories
phases.why_md:
Most failed projects fail before the first line of code: nobody wrote down what "done" means. A shop
adds a second question that costs real money when it is skipped: **what could go wrong with an
order?** The same bag sold twice, a customer charged twice, a "payment succeeded" message that nobody
sent. A short, testable requirements document with an explicit threat list gives every test a reason
to exist, lets you say *no* to scope creep, and is the first thing an interviewer asks about. AI
assistants are great at drafting requirements, and just as good at inventing requirements nobody asked
for. Your job is to keep the ones you can test.
objectives: Turn a one-paragraph brief into numbered **functional** (FR) and **measurable non-functional** (NFR) requirements.
Map personas (and one system: the payment provider) to **roles** and write down who may do what.
List at least six **threats** (abuse cases and failure cases) and the requirement that answers each.
Write 8–10 **user stories** with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and create them as GitHub Issues.
Write an explicit **out-of-scope** list and a **back-of-the-envelope estimate** for a festival sale.

steps.title: Read the brief and the contract
steps.content_md:
> *Build ShopFlow: the backend of a small Indian online shop. Anyone can browse and search the
> catalog. Customers register, keep a cart (with coupons), check out and pay through a payment
> provider that calls us back. The owner adds products, manages stock and ships paid orders. Prices are
> in rupees and must be exact. It must never sell more than it has, never create two orders for one
> checkout, and only believe the payment provider about payments. AI may help the owner write
> descriptions and help shoppers search in plain language, but the shop must work without it. It must
> run on a laptop for free.*

Open `spec/openapi.yaml`. The HTTP contract is **given** so the three tracks stay compatible; your
requirements must be consistent with it (status codes, limits, the `problem+json` error format, which
endpoints declare `security: bearerAuth`, the `Idempotency-Key` and `X-Signature` headers).

steps.title: Personas and the permission matrix
steps.content_md:
Write at least three personas, e.g. *Priya, who shops on her phone*; *Kabir, the owner*; and
**fakepay**, the payment provider: not a person, but an actor with its own way to authenticate (a
signature). Then fill a matrix: rows = actions (browse, see an inactive product, edit a product, use a
cart, check out, see my order, see someone else's order, ship an order, read the outbox, call the
webhook), columns = anonymous, CUSTOMER, ADMIN. Every "no" in this table becomes a test in Phase 3.
Decide now what a refused request returns: `401` (not logged in), `403` (logged in, not allowed) or
`404` (you should not even learn that it exists, e.g. someone else's order).

steps.title: Functional requirements
steps.content_md:
In `spec/requirements.md` write FR-1 … FR-n as "The system shall …" statements. Each needs a number
or a status code, so a test can check it. Bad: *"Shipping is cheap."* Good: *"Shipping is 4 900 paise,
free when the subtotal after the discount is at least 99 900 paise."* Cover registration and login,
roles, the catalog (browse, search, admin edits, stock), money, the cart and coupons, checkout, orders
and their states, the payment webhook, the outbox, the two AI helpers, errors and health.

Money deserves its own requirement. Write down **how amounts are represented** (integer paise
everywhere) and **how a percentage discount is rounded** (down, to the paisa). If you leave this open,
the three tracks will disagree by one paisa and every test that compares totals becomes flaky.

steps.title: Non-functional requirements and threats
steps.content_md:
Cover money correctness, overselling, duplicates, security, performance, availability, privacy, cost
and portability. Make each one measurable: *"under 20 parallel checkouts for the last unit exactly
one succeeds"*, *"catalog reads answer in < 200 ms p95 on a free-tier instance"*, *"checkout works
when the LLM is down"*.

Then the threat list. For each abuse or failure case, name the requirement that stops it:

| Threat | Answer |
|---|---|
| A shopper calls `/payments/webhook` herself with "payment succeeded" | HMAC signature on the raw body (FR-13) |
| The customer double-taps "Pay", or the app retries after a timeout | `Idempotency-Key` + a unique constraint (FR-11) |
| Two customers buy the last unit at the same moment | guarded stock decrement + `CHECK (stock >= 0)` (FR-11, NFR-2) |
| A new user sends `"role":"ADMIN"` when registering | registration ignores `role` (FR-1) |
| Someone walks through `/orders/1`, `/orders/2`, … | someone else's order is `404` (FR-12) |
| The order is paid but the warehouse never hears about it | transactional outbox (FR-14) |

steps.title: User stories → GitHub Issues
steps.content_md:
For each story use the **User story** issue template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user_story.yml`). It asks
for the story, the acceptance criteria and the Phase 3 milestone. Label them `user-story`. With the
GitHub CLI:
```bash
gh issue create --template user_story.yml      # or use the web UI: Issues → New issue
```
Write at least one acceptance criterion per story that describes a **refusal or a failure** (wrong
role, someone else's order, not enough stock, a redelivered webhook), not only the happy path.

steps.title: Out of scope + estimates
steps.content_md:
List what v1 will **not** do (real payment providers, actual refunds, GST invoices, images, reviews,
a front end, e-mails, multi-currency…). Then estimate: products, visitors/day, orders/day, the peak of
a festival sale (× 10 for two hours), read:write ratio, requests/second at peak and storage per year.
Write one sentence on what the numbers mean for the design (spoiler: one PostgreSQL instance is
plenty; the hard part is **correctness under concurrency**, not scale).

steps.title: Commit
steps.content_md:
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-1-requirements
git add spec/requirements.md AI_LOG.md
git commit -m "docs(spec): requirements, threats and user stories"
git push -u origin docs/phase-1-requirements      # open a PR, wait for CI, merge
```
Compare with the reference: `git diff phase-0-end phase-1-end -- spec/requirements.md`.

ai_prompts.title: Draft requirements from the brief
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a product brief: <paste the brief> and an OpenAPI contract: <paste spec/openapi.yaml>.
Draft numbered functional requirements ("The system shall ...") and measurable non-functional
requirements for v1. Every requirement must be testable and consistent with the contract (quote the

quiz.q: Which requirement is testable?
options: "A PERCENT coupon's discount is subtotal × percent / 100 rounded down to the paisa, capped at max_discount_paise."
quiz.explanation: It has an exact rule a unit test can check with numbers. The others need a measurable threshold first.

quiz.q: A logged-in CUSTOMER requests `GET /api/v1/orders/42`, which belongs to someone else. What should the API answer?
quiz.explanation: `403` would confirm that order 42 exists (and tell a competitor how many orders you have). For resources the caller should not even know about, `404` leaks nothing.

quiz.q: Why does the payment webhook need a signature instead of a bearer token?
options: The caller is the provider's server, not a user; an HMAC of the raw body proves the message came from someone who knows the shared secret and was not changed
The signature makes the request faster
quiz.explanation: Without it anyone could POST "payment succeeded" for their own unpaid order. The signature covers the exact bytes of the body, so it also detects tampering.

quiz.q: Why store money as integer paise rather than rupees in a float?
options: Floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3), so totals and threshold checks drift
quiz.explanation: Integers in the smallest unit are exact in every language and in SQL. Rupees only appear when formatting for humans.

quiz.q: Your estimate says ~60 orders/day, 600 on a festival day. What does that mean for the design?
options: You need a message queue and microservices
One PostgreSQL instance is plenty; spend the effort on correctness under concurrency
You must shard the orders table
You need a cache in front of checkout
quiz.explanation: Even the peak is a few checkouts per minute. What breaks a small shop is two requests at the same instant for the last unit, not volume.

quiz.q: An AI draft adds "FR-20: customers can pay with saved cards". What do you do?
options: Keep it, more features are better
Remove it (or move it to out of scope): it is not in the brief, and storing card data brings PCI DSS obligations
Add a cards table to the schema
Ask the AI if it is needed
quiz.explanation: Requirements come from the brief and the contract, not from the assistant's idea of a typical shop. Card data should never touch ShopFlow at all; log the rejection in `AI_LOG.md`.

A permission matrix with a non-human actor, and the 401 vs 403 vs 404 decision.
Threat modelling that includes failure cases: double clicks, races and redelivered messages.
Pinning down money rules (unit, rounding) before any code exists.
User stories with refusal criteria, tracked as GitHub Issues, and estimates that keep the design simple.

phases.title: Design (architecture, money, concurrency, DB schema, API contract)
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: architecture, money, concurrency, database schema, API contract
phases.why_md:
Design is where you make the expensive decisions on purpose: how money is represented, what stops two
customers buying the last unit, what happens when a checkout request is retried, how a payment
callback is trusted, and how other systems learn that an order was paid without ever losing that
message. Writing them down as diagrams and **Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)** lets a reviewer
follow your reasoning in minutes. The SQL schema is the one artefact shared by all three tracks, so a
mistake here costs three times, and a missing constraint is an overselling bug waiting for a sale day.
objectives: Draw context, container and sequence diagrams (checkout, payment webhook) and the order state machine in Mermaid.
Write five ADRs: money as integer paise, guarded stock decrement, optimistic locking for product edits, idempotent checkout + webhook de-duplication, and a transactional outbox.
Design the PostgreSQL schema and write it as migration `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`.
Read the given OpenAPI contract and map each endpoint to a requirement.
Watch your track's migrator apply V1 on start-up and prove the constraints by breaking them.

steps.title: Diagrams in `spec/architecture.md`
steps.content_md:
Mermaid is text, so it diffs and reviews like code. Start with a container diagram:
```text
flowchart TB
    client([Storefront, mobile app, curl]) --> app["ShopFlow app :8080"]
    pay([Payment provider]) -- "signed webhook" --> app
    app -- "SQL (source of truth)" --> pg[("PostgreSQL 16")]
    app -. "optional, timeout + fallback" .-> llm[("LLM endpoint")]
```
Wrap it in a code fence with the language `mermaid` and preview it on GitHub or in VS Code (extension
"Markdown Preview Mermaid Support"). Then draw:
1. **Checkout** with an `Idempotency-Key`: first call, a retry with the same key, two customers racing
   for the last unit.
2. **Payment webhook**: a valid event, the same event redelivered, a bad signature, a success that
   arrives after the customer cancelled.
3. **The order state machine** (`stateDiagram-v2`): PENDING_PAYMENT, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED
   and the action on every arrow.

steps.title: ADRs
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/adr/0000-template.md` five times:
1. `0001-money-as-integer-paise.md`: floats vs decimal types vs integers in the smallest unit. How is a
   percentage rounded? What does the JSON look like?
2. `0002-guarded-stock-decrement.md`: read-check-write vs `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` vs one guarded
   `UPDATE … WHERE stock >= :q`. What does "0 rows updated" mean?
3. `0003-optimistic-locking-for-products.md`: last-write-wins vs a `version` column. Why must stock
   changes **not** bump the version?
4. `0004-idempotent-checkout-and-webhook-dedup.md`: where is the key stored, what makes two identical
   requests racing safe, how is a redelivered webhook recognised?
5. `0005-transactional-outbox.md`: publish-after-commit vs 2PC vs an outbox table. What delivery
   guarantee do consumers get, and what must they do about it?

Each ADR is one page: context, options with pros/cons, decision, consequences.

steps.title: Schema → `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`
steps.content_md:
Requirements to satisfy:
- `users`: unique, lower-case `email` (enforce lower case with a `CHECK`), `password_hash`, `role`
  restricted by a `CHECK` to CUSTOMER/ADMIN.
- `products`: unique `sku`, `price_paise BIGINT` with a range `CHECK`, `stock` with
  **`CHECK (stock >= 0)`**, `version`, `active`, and a **generated** `tsvector` column for full-text
  search with a GIN index. A partial index on active products.
- `coupons` (PERCENT/FLAT, optional cap and minimum) seeded with the demo codes `SAVE10`, `FLAT100`,
  `EXPIRED5`.
- `carts` + `cart_items` (one cart per user, quantity `CHECK` 1–10).
- `orders` with every money column, `CHECK (total_paise = subtotal_paise - discount_paise +
  shipping_paise)`, a status `CHECK`, and **`UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key)`**.
- `order_items` with SKU, name and unit price **copied** from the product.
- `payments` (one per order) and `payment_events` (the webhook event id is the primary key).
- `outbox_events` (JSONB payload, nullable `published_at`, a partial index on pending rows).

Name every constraint (`uq_users_email`, `ck_products_stock`, …) so error handling and tests can refer
to it. Never edit a migration after it is merged. Add `V2__…` instead (you will do that in Phase 7).

steps.title: Watch the migrator apply it
steps.content_md:
Every track runs the same tiny migrator at start-up (no Flyway/Alembic, so the three tracks can share
one SQL file). It takes a PostgreSQL advisory lock, so two instances never migrate at the same time,
and applies each file in its own transaction. Start your app (`make run`) and inspect the result:
```bash
docker compose exec postgres psql -U shopflow -d shopflow -c '\d products' -c 'select * from schema_migrations'
```

against an old schema.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
Python: `tracks/python/app/db.py` → `run_migrations()`, called in the FastAPI `lifespan` in `app/main.py`.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->

ai_prompts.title: Mermaid sequence diagram for an idempotent checkout
ai_prompts.prompt:
Write a Mermaid sequenceDiagram with participants Customer, App, Postgres for an idempotent checkout:
(1) POST /checkout with Idempotency-Key k1: look up an order by (user, k1), none found; price the cart in
integer paise; BEGIN; for each line UPDATE products SET stock = stock - q WHERE id = ? AND stock >= q
(0 rows -> ROLLBACK, 409); INSERT order, lines, a PENDING payment and an outbox event; empty the cart;
COMMIT; 201. (2) The same request again: return the stored order with 200. (3) Two identical requests
racing: the UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key) constraint lets one win; the loser returns the winner's
order. Use alt blocks and keep messages short.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: pasting it into https://mermaid.live (it must render), then walking through each branch against FR-11, NFR-2 and NFR-3. Check that the stock check and the decrement are **one** statement (not a SELECT followed by an UPDATE) and that nothing is written outside the transaction.

<paste FR-1..18 and NFR-1..3>. Point out missing constraints, wrong types for money, missing or useless
indexes, anything that would allow overselling, a second order for the same idempotency key, a webhook
applied twice, or an order whose total does not add up. Do not add tables for out-of-scope features.

ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`): it must use `idx_orders_user`, not a `Seq Scan` (insert a few thousand rows first with `generate_series`). Reject any suggestion to store money as `NUMERIC` in rupees *and* integers: one representation only.

UPDATE (pessimistic locking) instead of a single guarded UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= :q. Then list when
pessimistic locking is genuinely better. Keep it under 250 words.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking each claim against your ADR-0002 (round trips, lock duration, deadlocks when two carts lock the same products in a different order, what happens on a crash) and recording the strongest counter-argument in the ADR's *Consequences*. deliverables.text: `spec/architecture.md` with context, container, checkout, webhook, state machine and ER diagrams that render on GitHub.
`spec/adr/0001…0005` accepted.
`spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`; the app applies it on start-up (`schema_migrations` has version 1).
Every OpenAPI path mapped to a requirement; the constraint experiments in Step 2.4 fail as expected.
Compare: `git diff phase-1-end phase-2-end --stat`.

quiz.q: Why is `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock >= 1` safe when `SELECT stock` followed by `UPDATE` is not?
options: The check and the write happen in one statement under the row lock, so two buyers cannot both see "1 left"
It does not need a transaction
quiz.explanation: With read-check-write, two requests can read 1 at the same time and both write 0. The guarded update makes the second one match 0 rows, which the code turns into `409 insufficient-stock`.

quiz.q: A 10 % coupon on a subtotal of 99 999 paise. What is the discount?
quiz.explanation: 99 999 × 10 / 100 = 9 999.9, rounded **down** to 9 999 paise in integer arithmetic (ADR-0001). The shop never gives away more than it advertised, and there is no fractional paisa anywhere.

quiz.q: Why is `UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key)` needed when the code already looks the key up first?
options: Two identical requests can both pass the lookup at the same moment; the constraint lets only one INSERT win
Keys must be unique across all users
PostgreSQL requires it for foreign keys
quiz.explanation: The lookup handles retries; the constraint handles races. The loser of the race catches the duplicate error and returns the winner's order instead.

quiz.q: Why does adjusting stock NOT increase the product's `version`?
options: Stock is not stored in the products table
Checkouts change stock constantly; bumping the version would make every admin edit during a sale fail with 409
Optimistic locking only works for text columns
The version is only for the outbox
quiz.explanation: Optimistic locking protects human edits from each other. Stock is protected differently (the guarded decrement), so it must not interfere.

quiz.q: The order is committed as PAID, then the process crashes before calling the message broker. With a transactional outbox, what happens?
options: The `order.paid` row was committed with the order; the relay publishes it later
quiz.explanation: The event is written in the same transaction as the state change, so they exist together or not at all. The price is at-least-once delivery: consumers de-duplicate on the event id.

quiz.q: Why are the product name and price copied into `order_items`?
options: An order must show what the customer actually bought and paid, even after the product is renamed or repriced
quiz.explanation: An order is a historical record (and the basis of an invoice). Products change; orders must not change with them.

recap: Diagrams-as-code with Mermaid: context, containers, sequences, a state machine, ER.
Money as integers in the smallest unit, with an explicit rounding rule.
Concurrency answers you can explain: a guarded update, a unique constraint, optimistic locking, compare-and-set state transitions.
Idempotency keys, webhook de-duplication and the transactional outbox as answers to unreliable networks.
Schema design with named constraints, CHECKs, generated columns, partial and GIN indexes.

phases.title: Implementation in milestones
phases.heading: Phase 3 · Implementation in five milestones
phases.why_md:
This is where a shop either keeps its promises or loses money. The tests are already written: they
describe every rule from Phase 1 (prices in paise, coupon caps, the cart limits, the order states, the
webhook) and every refusal (wrong role, someone else's order, not enough stock). Working test-first,
one milestone at a time, keeps you honest and gives you a green bar to show for each step. It is also
where AI assistants are most tempting and most dangerous: they write plausible checkout code fast, and
the bugs they leave (a read-then-write stock check, a webhook that trusts its body, a float in a
price) only show up on the busiest day of the year.
objectives: Implement ShopFlow in **your** track in five milestones: **M1** validation + money · **M2** auth (bcrypt, JWT, roles) and webhook signatures · **M3** catalog, full-text search, optimistic locking and the two AI helpers · **M4** cart and coupons · **M5** idempotent checkout, the order state machine, the payment webhook and the outbox.
Use the pending list to work test-first.
Keep the HTTP layer thin and the business logic (including authorisation) in framework-free services.
Review AI-generated checkout code critically and catch a planted race with a test.

Un-pend **security**, **auth** and **api-auth**. Build it in this order:
1. `PasswordHasher`: bcrypt with the configured cost (tests use 4 so they stay fast). `verify` must
   return `false`, not throw, on a malformed hash, and must still do the work for an unknown user
   (the starter postponed the dummy hash in the constructor; restore it).
2. `TokenService`: issue an HS256 JWT (`sub`, `role`, `iss`, `iat`, `exp = now + 3600 s` from the
   injected clock) and verify it with the **algorithm pinned**.
3. Webhook signatures: `sign` = `"sha256=" + hex(HMAC-SHA256(secret, raw body))`; `verify` compares in
   **constant time**.
4. `AuthService`: register (always CUSTOMER), login (same `401` for unknown e-mail and wrong password),
   `me`, `ensure_admin` (the start-up bootstrap: until it works the app starts without an admin) and
   `authenticate`/`optional` for the `Authorization` header.

steps.title: M3: catalog, search and the AI helpers (FR-4 … FR-6, FR-15, FR-16, NFR-6)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **catalog**, **api-products**, **ai** and **api-ai**.
* `CatalogService`: admin-only create (`409 sku-taken` on a duplicate), `get` (inactive products are
  `404` for everyone but admins), `update` with **optimistic locking** (ADR-0003), `adjust_stock` with
  the **guarded** statement (ADR-0002), and `list`/`search` with keyset pagination: ask the repository
  for `limit + 1` rows; if the extra row exists, `nextCursor` is the cursor of the last row **shown**.
* The repository: `WHERE active AND id > :after [AND search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', :q)]
  … ORDER BY id LIMIT :n`. Placeholders only, never string concatenation: the filters come from the
  query string.
* **Description drafts:** the template writer is deterministic and its wording is checked by the tests;
  the LLM writer sends the product facts between `<product>` tags. `DescriptionService` falls back to
  the template on **any** exception and says so (`fallback: true`). Drafts are returned, never saved.
* **Search assist:** the rule parser turns *"running shoes under 3k in stock"* into
  `{terms:[running], category: shoes, maxPricePaise: 300000, inStock: true}` with the regexes at the
  top of the file, in a fixed order. The LLM parser asks for JSON and `parse_filters` validates the
  answer **like untrusted user input** (unknown category, a price that is a boolean, six terms → throw →
  fallback). Prompt injection in the search box can then at worst produce a strange but *valid* filter.

```bash
ADMIN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"email":"admin@shopflow.local","password":"admin-password-123"}' | sed 's/.*"accessToken":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/')
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/products -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"sku":"SHOE-RUN-1","name":"Trail running shoes","category":"shoes","pricePaise":249900,"stock":3,"description":"Light and grippy."}'
curl -s 'localhost:8080/api/v1/search/assist?q=running%20shoes%20under%203000%20in%20stock'
```
Optional, with a local model: `docker compose --profile ollama up -d`, pull `llama3.2:1b`, run your track
with `AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1` and compare the answers. Then stop Ollama
and call it again: `provider` becomes `rules` and `fallback` `true`, with a `200`.

steps.title: M4: cart and coupons (FR-8 … FR-10)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **cart** and **api-cart**. The cart is priced **on every read** with current prices, so a price
change reaches carts immediately and the client never sends a price (threat T6). `set_item` *sets* the
quantity (it does not add), refuses more than the current stock, and refuses a 21st different product;
removing a line that is not there is fine (idempotent). A coupon that exists but whose minimum is not
met stays on the cart with `couponApplied: false`: the customer sees why there is no discount.
```bash
curl -s -X PUT localhost:8080/api/v1/cart/items/SHOE-RUN-1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $PRIYA" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"quantity":1}'
curl -s -X PUT localhost:8080/api/v1/cart/coupon -H "Authorization: Bearer $PRIYA" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"code":"SAVE10"}'      # discount 20000 (the ₹200 cap), shipping 0
```

steps.title: M5: checkout, orders, payments and the outbox (FR-11 … FR-14, NFR-2, NFR-3)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **orders**, **payments** and **api-orders**. Three pieces:
1. **Checkout** (ADR-0004): look the `Idempotency-Key` up first (replay → the same order,
   `replayed=true`), then price the cart and call `place_order`, which does **everything in one
   transaction**: a guarded decrement per line, the order with copied lines, the PENDING payment, the
   `order.placed` event, and an empty cart. Not enough stock for any line → nothing at all changes. A
   duplicate-key error means an identical request won the race: return its order.
2. **The state machine**: `next_status(current, action)` from the transitions table, and
   `transition_for` adds the side effects (an outbox event per new status, `refund.requested` when a PAID
   order is cancelled, restock on cancel). The repository applies it as a **compare-and-set**
   (`… WHERE id = ? AND status = :from`), so a customer's cancel and the webhook cannot both win.
3. **The webhook**: verify the signature on the **raw bytes** first (parsing and re-serialising JSON
   changes the bytes and breaks the HMAC), then the event id, type and payment id; a known event id is a
   `duplicate`; a success after a cancel keeps the order cancelled and asks for a refund.

Then the relay: `publish_pending` publishes in id order and stops at the first failure (ADR-0005).
```bash
ORDER=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/checkout -H "Authorization: Bearer $PRIYA" -H 'Idempotency-Key: try-it-0001')
echo "$ORDER"            # 201, PENDING_PAYMENT; run the same command again: 200, same id
PAY=$(echo "$ORDER" | sed 's/.*"payment":{"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/')
BODY="{\"id\":\"evt_try_0001\",\"type\":\"payment.succeeded\",\"paymentId\":\"$PAY\"}"
SIG=$(printf '%s' "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac 'local-webhook-secret-change-me-0123456789' | sed 's/^.* //')
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/payments/webhook -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -H "X-Signature: sha256=$SIG" -d "$BODY"         # processed; send it again: duplicate
curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/outbox -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN"
```

steps.title: Review the AI's code (exercise)
steps.content_md:
An assistant produced this checkout (pseudo-code). Find the bugs **before** reading on, then point to
the test that catches them.
```text
for line in cart.lines:
    product = repo.findProduct(line.sku)
    if product.stock < line.quantity: raise 409
    repo.updateStock(product.id, product.stock - line.quantity)
order = repo.insertOrder(user, lines, total = sum(line.price * line.quantity) * (1 - coupon.percent / 100.0))
cart.clear()
```
Three bugs: the stock check is **read-then-write** outside a transaction (two customers both see 1
left; a crash halfway leaves stock decremented without an order); the total uses a **float** (and the
client-side `line.price`); and there is **no idempotency key**, so a retry creates a second order. The
unit tests *"checkout is idempotent per key"* and *"a coupon rounds the discount down"* fail against it,
and in Phase 4 the integration test *"concurrent checkouts never oversell"* shows the race. Note in
`AI_LOG.md` how you found it.

quiz.q: Why must the services use an injected clock?
options: It is faster than the system clock
Tests can move time forward to check token expiry (and, in v1.1, payment windows) without sleeping
quiz.explanation: `clock.advance(minutes=61)` makes "expired access token" deterministic. Code that calls `now()` directly can only be tested by waiting an hour.

quiz.q: Why is the webhook signature checked on the raw request body, before parsing JSON?
options: The HMAC covers exact bytes; re-serialised JSON can differ (spacing, key order), and unverified input should not be processed at all
quiz.explanation: Verify first, then parse. The HTTP layer keeps the raw bytes for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: Why compare the signature with `hmac.compare_digest` / `MessageDigest.isEqual` / `timingSafeEqual` instead of `==`?
options: `==` stops at the first different character, so response times reveal how much of a forged signature was right
`==` does not work on hex strings
The constant-time functions also verify the JSON
quiz.explanation: Timing attacks recover a secret value byte by byte. Constant-time comparison removes the signal.

quiz.q: The same `Idempotency-Key` arrives twice at the same moment. What makes sure only one order is created?
options: The first lookup of the key
The unique constraint on (user_id, idempotency_key): the loser's INSERT fails and it returns the winner's order
The HTTP server drops the second request

options: Returns 409 so the provider stops retrying

options: Parse the sentence with the rules, answer `200` with `provider: "rules"` and `fallback: true`

quiz.explanation: The AI is an optional layer on a deterministic baseline (NFR-6). Shoppers can always search, and `fallback` makes the degradation visible.

options: Reading the stock and writing `stock - quantity` back in a separate statement
Looking the product up by SKU
quiz.explanation: Two concurrent checkouts both read 1 and both write 0. A guarded `UPDATE … WHERE stock >= :q` in the checkout transaction closes the race.

phases.title: Testing (unit, integration, security, coverage)
phases.heading: Phase 4 · Testing: integration, security and concurrency tests, coverage gate
phases.why_md:
Unit tests with in-memory fakes prove your logic. They cannot prove that your SQL is valid, that the
database really refuses negative stock, that a failed checkout leaves **nothing** behind, or that ten
customers racing for the last three units really get exactly three orders. Integration tests against a
**real** PostgreSQL do. A coverage gate then stops the suite from quietly rotting. Together they let you
change code (or accept an AI's refactor) without fear, which is exactly what you need before CI in Phase 5.
objectives: Explain the test pyramid for ShopFlow: unit (fast, many), integration (real database), smoke (black-box, few).
Run the integration suite against the Compose database using a **separate** test database.

Prove money, security and concurrency behaviour at the database level: hashed passwords, unique constraints, all-or-nothing checkout, no overselling under parallel checkouts, one order per idempotency key, a webhook delivered twice at once applied once.
Enforce ≥ 85 % line coverage locally and understand what the number does and does not mean.

steps.title: Read the money, security and concurrency tests
steps.content_md:
Open the integration file and find these cases. Each maps to a requirement:
- **migrations are recorded and the demo coupons are seeded** (FR-10, Phase 2).
- **passwords are hashed and e-mails unique** (FR-1, NFR-4): the test reads `users.password_hash` with
  SQL and checks for a bcrypt prefix; a duplicate e-mail fails even as a direct insert.
- **SKU uniqueness and optimistic locking in the database** (FR-5, ADR-0003).
- **full-text search stems and filters** ("shoe" finds "Shoes") and **keyset pagination over the real
  index** (FR-4).
- **the database refuses negative stock** (`ck_products_stock`, NFR-2): even an UPDATE by hand fails.
- **checkout is one transaction** (FR-11): a cart whose *second* line is out of stock leaves the first
  product's stock, the orders table, the payments and the outbox exactly as they were.
- **concurrent checkouts never oversell** (NFR-2, ADR-0002): many customers check out the last units
  at once; exactly `stock` of them get `201`, the rest `409 insufficient-stock`, and stock ends at 0.
- **concurrent retries with one key create one order** (NFR-3, ADR-0004).
- **a webhook delivered twice at once is processed exactly once** (FR-13).
- **cancel restocks and the relay marks events published** (FR-12, FR-14, ADR-0005).
- **the admin is bootstrapped from the environment** (FR-3) and **health reports DOWN when the
  database is unreachable** (FR-18).

steps.title: Prove one test can fail
steps.content_md:
A test you have never seen fail proves nothing. Pick the overselling test and break the code on purpose
in a scratch branch: change your guarded decrement so it reads the stock first and writes
`stock - quantity` in a second statement (or simply drop `AND stock >= :q` from the `UPDATE`). Run
`make test-integration` (repeat a few times if needed): it must go red, for the right reason (more
`201`s than units, or the CHECK constraint firing as a `500`). Restore the line. Do the same for the
`status = :from` condition of the order transition and the webhook test.

stock 3, exactly 3 orders are created and stock ends at 0. Here is my test setup: <paste>. Write the

quiz.q: Which bug can ONLY an integration test catch here?
options: A wrong error message for a too-long product name
A typo in the `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - :q WHERE … AND stock >= :q` statement
A coupon cap that is applied in the wrong order
quiz.explanation: Unit tests use the in-memory repositories, so the SQL never runs there. The other bugs live in pure logic and are covered by unit tests.

quiz.q: How does the integration suite prove that passwords are not stored in clear text?
options: It reads `users.password_hash` with SQL and checks it is a bcrypt hash, not the password
It logs in with the password
It checks the HTTP response does not contain the password
quiz.explanation: The response and the database are different places a secret can leak. Only a test that looks at the stored row proves the storage requirement.

quiz.q: Why does the concurrency test need real parallel requests?
options: The overselling bug only appears when two checkouts read the same stock before either writes
To test the connection pool size
quiz.explanation: Sequentially, the second checkout already sees the lower stock. The guarded statement under PostgreSQL's row lock is what makes the parallel case safe.

quiz.q: Your coverage is 93 %. What does that prove?
options: The code has no security bugs
93 % of lines executed during the tests. It says nothing about whether the assertions are meaningful
The integration tests are not needed
quiz.explanation: Coverage finds *untested* code; it cannot find *wrong* tests. Use it as a floor, not a target.

quiz.q: Why break the code on purpose and watch a test fail?
options: A test that cannot fail gives false confidence; seeing it go red proves it checks the behaviour
quiz.explanation: It is a cheap form of mutation testing. Assistants often write tests that pass against any implementation.

phases.title: CI with GitHub Actions
phases.heading: Phase 5 · Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
phases.why_md:
"It passed on my machine" is not evidence. CI runs the same checks on a clean machine for every push
and pull request, so a broken change never reaches `main`. It is also the cheapest code reviewer you
will ever have. In this phase you grow the starter workflow into a real pipeline: path filters, a
reusable workflow, service containers for integration tests, caching, a coverage artefact and one
required status check.

Every keyword used here is explained slowly in **[docs/github-actions-explained.md](github-actions-explained.md)**.
Read it side by side with the YAML.
objectives: Explain triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, matrices, caching and artefacts.
Write a **reusable workflow** (`workflow_call`) that runs one track's full check, and call it three times.
Run integration tests in CI with a PostgreSQL **service container**.
Skip unaffected tracks with a **path filter**, and still have a single required check (`ci-ok`).
Validate the OpenAPI contract in CI and enable **Dependabot**.
Protect `main` so a PR cannot be merged while CI is red.

steps.title: Read the starter workflow
steps.content_md:
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It is a **matrix** over `[java, python, typescript]`; each matrix job
sets up one toolchain (`if: matrix.track == 'java'`), then runs `make install`, `make lint` and `make test`.
The same Makefile targets exist in every track, so CI does not need three different scripts.

steps.title: Create the reusable workflow
steps.content_md:
Create `.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml` with `on: workflow_call` and an input `track`. Give its job:
- `services:` `postgres:16-alpine` with a health check and a published port,
- `env:` `TEST_DATABASE_URL` pointing at `localhost`,
- the setup steps from the starter, then `make install lint test`,
- a step that creates `shopflow_test` (`docker exec ${{ job.services.postgres.id }} psql …`),
- `make coverage` (unit + integration + the 85 % gate),
- `actions/upload-artifact@v4` for the coverage report (`if: always()`).

steps.title: Rewrite `ci.yml` as an orchestrator
steps.content_md:
1. A `changes` job with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` that outputs `docs`, `shared`, `java`, `python`, `typescript`.
2. A `contract` job (only when shared files or docs change): `pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml`,
   `shellcheck` on `scripts/*.sh` and `python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check` (the course export must match `docs/`).
3. Three jobs `java`, `python`, `typescript`, each `uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml`
   with `if:` on its path output.
4. A final `ci-ok` job with `if: always()` and `needs:` on all of them that fails when any result is
   `failure` or `cancelled`. Skipped is fine.

The reference is at `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

steps.title: Lint your workflows before pushing
steps.content_md:
```bash
# https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint  (Go binary; also available via Homebrew / Docker)
go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest
actionlint                       # run from the repo root
```
`actionlint` catches typos in expressions, unknown inputs, bad `needs` and shell bugs (via shellcheck)
before GitHub ever sees them.

steps.title: Dependabot
steps.content_md:
Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with one entry per ecosystem: `maven` in `/tracks/java`, `pip` in
`/tracks/python`, `npm` in `/tracks/typescript`, and `github-actions` in `/`. Group minor + patch updates
so you get one PR per ecosystem per week.

steps.title: Protect `main`
steps.content_md:
In your fork: **Settings → Branches → Add branch ruleset** (or classic rule) for `main`:
- Require a pull request before merging.
- Require status checks to pass → add **`ci-ok`** (it appears after the first run).
- Block force pushes.

Because skipped jobs count as success, a docs-only PR still gets a green `ci-ok` quickly.

steps.title: Prove it works
steps.content_md:
Open a PR that breaks one test in **one** track: only that track's job runs (path filter) and `ci-ok`
goes red, so the merge button is blocked. Fix it and watch it go green. Then open a PR that only touches
`spec/openapi.yaml`: all jobs run, because a contract change affects every track.

quiz.q: What does `on: workflow_call` mean?
options: The workflow runs when someone calls the repository's API
The workflow can be used as a reusable workflow by other workflows (`jobs.<id>.uses`)
The workflow runs on every push
The workflow can only be run manually
quiz.explanation: A reusable workflow is like a function: it declares `inputs`, and the caller passes them with `with:`.

quiz.q: Why is `ci-ok` the only required check instead of every job?
options: GitHub allows only one required check
With path filters some jobs are skipped; one aggregator job gives a stable name that is green when nothing failed
Reusable workflows cannot be required checks
quiz.explanation: Required checks are matched by name. An aggregator with `if: always()` survives jobs being skipped or renamed.

quiz.q: How do integration tests reach PostgreSQL in CI?
options: They connect to a free cloud database
A `services:` container runs next to the job and its port is published on `localhost`
Docker Compose is started inside the test
quiz.explanation: Service containers live for one job, are health-checked before steps start, and are thrown away afterwards.

quiz.q: What does `cache: npm` (or `maven`/`pip`) in a setup action do?
options: Restores the package download cache keyed by a hash of the lock file, so installs are faster
quiz.explanation: The key changes when `package-lock.json` / `pom.xml` / `requirements-dev.txt` changes, so you never get stale dependencies.

quiz.q: Which default `permissions` block is safest for a CI workflow that only reads code?
quiz.explanation: Least privilege. Jobs that need more (e.g. pushing images) ask for it explicitly, as `deploy.yml` does in Phase 6.

Reusable workflows with inputs, and an orchestrator workflow that calls them.

phases.title: Containerise, deliver, and (optionally) deploy to a free tier
phases.heading: Phase 6 · Containerise, deliver and (optionally) deploy
phases.why_md:
A container image is the unit you actually ship: the same bytes run on your laptop, in CI and in
the cloud. In this phase you write a production-grade Dockerfile, run the whole stack with one
command, prove it with a black-box smoke test, and publish versioned images to GitHub Container
Registry (GHCR) automatically on every release tag. Deploying to the cloud is **optional**: everything
graded in this phase works offline on your laptop.
objectives: Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile with a `HEALTHCHECK` for your track.
Add your app to `docker-compose.yml` as a profile and start the stack with `docker compose --profile <track> up`.
Run the language-agnostic smoke test against your container (and against the other tracks' images).
Add a Docker build + smoke job to CI.
Write `deploy.yml`: on a `v*.*.*` tag, build and push images to GHCR; optionally trigger a Render deploy that is **skipped gracefully** when no secret is configured.
Cut release **v1.0.0** with a CHANGELOG entry.

steps.title: The Dockerfile (build context = repository root)
steps.content_md:
All tracks copy the shared migrations into the image, so the build context is the repo root and the
Dockerfile lives in the track: `docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile .`. Rules:

steps.title: Compose profiles: one command for the whole stack
steps.content_md:
Add a service per track to `docker-compose.yml` under a **profile**, sharing one block of environment
variables (a YAML anchor `x-app-env`), `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, and port
`${APP_PORT:-8080}:8080`. Inside Compose the app reaches the database as `postgres:5432`, not `localhost`.
The Compose file sets **local-only** values for `JWT_SECRET` and the first admin
(`admin@shopflow.local` / `admin-password-123`) through `${VAR:-default}`, so `docker compose up` works out
of the box. A real deployment sets its own values: the defaults are public, in this repository.
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

steps.title: Smoke test (the same for every track)
steps.content_md:
```bash
scripts/smoke-test.sh                      # default http://localhost:8080
```
It checks 73 behaviours with only `bash`, `curl` and `openssl`: health, registration (the `role`
field is ignored), duplicate e-mail, `problem+json` errors, login, `/me` with and without a token, the
catalog, categories and search assist, then (logged in as the Compose admin) creating a product, `403`
for customers, optimistic locking (`409`), a guarded stock move, a description draft, the cart and a
coupon (with the ₹200 cap and free shipping), checkout **twice with the same Idempotency-Key** (one
order), someone else's order (`404`), a **signed** webhook, the same webhook again (`duplicate`), a
forged signature (`401`), shipping (a SHIPPED order can no longer be cancelled), a cancel that
restocks, and the outbox relay. It creates
its own uniquely named customers and product (deactivated at the end), so it is safe to run
repeatedly.
Against a deployment, pass the admin credentials as `SMOKE_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SMOKE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`. If you
cannot, `SMOKE_ALLOW_NO_ADMIN=true` turns the admin-dependent block into one `SKIP` instead of failures.
Because the contract is shared, try another track's
image against the same database: `docker compose stop app-<yours>` and `docker compose --profile python up -d`.
Same results. Also run the AI fallback check:
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=1000 docker compose --profile <track> up -d --wait
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh      # the description draft and search assist report fallback: true
```

steps.title: CI: build the image and smoke-test it
steps.content_md:
Add a `docker` job (matrix over tracks) to `ci.yml`: `docker/setup-buildx-action`,
`docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` and the GitHub Actions layer cache (`cache-from/to: type=gha`),
then `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --no-build --wait`, the smoke test, logs on failure and `down -v`.

steps.title: Continuous delivery to GHCR: `deploy.yml`
steps.content_md:
Trigger on `push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]`. The job needs `permissions: packages: write` and logs in to
`ghcr.io` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`; no personal token required. Image names must be lower-case
(the org is `AICanCode-org`), so compute `ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/shopflow-<track>`.
`docker/metadata-action` turns tag `v1.0.0` into image tags `1.0.0`, `1.0`, `sha-<short>` and `latest`.
Read `docs/github-actions-explained.md` §9–§12 for every detail.

steps.title: Release v1.0.0
steps.content_md:
```bash
# update CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" items under "## [1.0.0] - <date>"
git commit -am "chore(release): v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "ShopFlow v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```
Watch **Actions → Deploy**: three images appear under your profile's **Packages**. New GHCR packages
are **private** by default. Make one public (Package settings → Change visibility) if a host should pull
it without credentials.

steps.title: OPTIONAL: deploy to a free tier
steps.content_md:
You do not need a cloud account to finish this course. If you want a public URL:

| Piece | Free option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App | **Render** web service from an *existing image* (`ghcr.io/<you>/shopflow-<track>:latest`) | Free instances spin down after 15 minutes without traffic; the next request takes about a minute (cold start). |
| PostgreSQL | **Neon** free tier | Use its connection string as `DATABASE_URL` and keep `?sslmode=require`. Java: if the string contains `channel_binding=require`, remove that parameter. Render's own free Postgres also works but **expires after 30 days**. |
| Secrets | Render env vars | Set your own `JWT_SECRET` (`openssl rand -base64 48`), `PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (`openssl rand -hex 32`), `ADMIN_EMAIL`, a strong `ADMIN_PASSWORD`. Never reuse the Compose defaults. |
| LLM | none (rules/template), or a free Gemini / Groq key | `AI_PROVIDER=llm`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` as Render env vars. Tell your users if their search sentences are sent to a hosted model. |

Free-tier limits change. Check each provider's pricing page before you rely on it. Fly.io is **not**
used: at the time of writing it needs a payment method and bills usage, with no free tier for new accounts.

To let CI deploy for you:
1. Render → your service → **Settings → Deploy Hook**: copy the URL.
2. GitHub → **Settings → Environments → New environment `production`** (optionally add yourself as a
   required reviewer). Add the **secret** `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` and the **variables** `RENDER_APP_URL`
   (e.g. `https://shopflow-xyz.onrender.com`) and `DEPLOY_TRACK` (`java`, `python` or `typescript`).
   Optionally add the secrets `SMOKE_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SMOKE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` / `SMOKE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` so
   the live smoke test also runs the admin, cart, checkout and payment steps.
3. Push a tag. The `render` job calls the hook with `imgURL=` set to the exact version, waits for
   `/health`, and runs the smoke test against the live URL. Without the secret the job prints a notice
   and **succeeds**, so forks without cloud accounts stay green.

`docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait` + `scripts/smoke-test.sh`: all checks pass, and `EXPECT_FALLBACK=true` passes with an unreachable LLM.
CI `docker` job green; `deploy.yml` pushed images to GHCR for tag `v1.0.0`.
`CHANGELOG.md` with `[1.0.0]`; `docs/runbook.md` with start/stop/rollback/rotate-secret steps.
Optional: a live URL in your README and a green `render` job.

quiz.q: Why do the Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source code?
options: So that the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the manifest changes
quiz.explanation: Layers are cached top-down; anything after a changed layer is rebuilt. Source changes often, dependencies rarely.

quiz.q: Inside Docker Compose, which `DATABASE_URL` host does the app use?
quiz.explanation: Each container has its own `localhost`. Compose gives services DNS names on a shared network.

quiz.q: Why does the image push use `${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}`?
options: GHCR image names must be lower-case and the org name `AICanCode-org` has capitals
quiz.explanation: `,,` is bash's lower-case expansion. `ghcr.io/AICanCode-org/...` would be rejected.

quiz.q: A fork has no `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` secret. What does the `render` job do on a tag push?
options: Prints a notice and succeeds; the image is still pushed to the fork's GHCR
Waits for someone to add the secret
quiz.explanation: Optional infrastructure must not make the pipeline red. Secrets are read into `env:` and tested with `if: env.X == ''`.

quiz.q: Why are free hosting instances slow on the first request after a while?
options: Idle instances are stopped to save cost and must boot again (cold start)
quiz.explanation: That is why the deploy job polls `/health` for up to 10 minutes before smoke-testing.

quiz.q: Why must a deployment never use the `JWT_SECRET` from `docker-compose.yml`?
options: It is public in the repository, so anyone could sign a valid ADMIN token for your API
quiz.explanation: Whoever knows an HS256 secret can mint any token. Defaults are for laptops; deployments get their own secret from the host's environment variables.

recap: Production Dockerfiles: multi-stage, layer caching, non-root, health checks, `.dockerignore`.
Compose profiles to run any track against the same dependencies with one command.
Black-box smoke tests that work for any implementation of a contract.
Image builds with layer caching in CI, and delivery to GHCR with the built-in token on version tags.
Optional, secret-gated deployment that degrades gracefully, plus free-tier trade-offs (cold starts, TLS URLs).
Semantic versioning and a CHANGELOG-driven release.

phases.title: Observability and maintenance
phases.heading: Phase 7 · Observability and maintenance (v1.1.0)
phases.why_md:
Shipping v1.0.0 is the start, not the end. In production you have to answer "is it working right now,
and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That needs three things: **logs** you can search,
**metrics** you can graph, and a **request ID** that ties a customer's complaint ("my order failed at
19:42") to log lines. ShopFlow also depends on something you do not control, an LLM, so you will run a
**game day** where the LLM hangs, measure what shoppers feel, and fix it with a **circuit breaker**.
Finally you make your first **maintenance change**, driven by a real business problem (abandoned
checkouts lock stock forever): a schema migration, a new admin job and a backward-compatible API
field, released safely as v1.1.0.
objectives: Give every request an `X-Request-ID` (reuse a safe incoming one, or generate a UUID) and put it in every log line.
Emit structured **JSON logs**: one object per line, one access-log line per request.
Expose `/metrics` in Prometheus text format with eight counters that are identical in every track.
Run a **game day**: make the LLM hang, measure search-assist latency, check the checkout path, write a short blameless post-mortem.
Add an LLM **circuit breaker** (3 failures in a row → open for 30 s → one half-open trial).
Ship a backward-compatible change: `V2__order_payment_window.sql`, a payment window on every order (`expiresAt`), the admin expiry job, OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
Review and merge one Dependabot PR.

steps.title: Request IDs
steps.content_md:
Rule (shared by all tracks): if the incoming `X-Request-ID` matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, echo it;
otherwise generate a UUID. Never echo arbitrary input: a header containing a newline could inject
fake log lines or headers.

<!-- track:java -->
A `OncePerRequestFilter` (`web/RequestIdFilter.java`) sets the response header, puts `requestId` in
the SLF4J **MDC** (so every log line in that request carries it) and logs one `shopflow.access` line
with `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` using the fluent API
`LOG.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", …).log()`. `@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` makes it the first
filter, so even a `401` or a `404` gets an ID (ShopFlow uses only `spring-security-crypto`, not the filter chain).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A Starlette middleware (`app/observability.py`) stores the ID in `request.state`, sets the response
header and logs one `shopflow.access` record with `extra={"fields": {...}}`. The middleware wraps the
whole app, so error responses (`400`, `401`, `404`) carry the header too.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Fastify has request IDs built in: `genReqId` (calling `incomingOrNewId()` from `src/observability.ts`)
with `requestIdHeader: false`, so we validate the incoming value ourselves, and a `LogController` with `requestIdLogLabel: "requestId"`.
An `onSend` hook copies `request.id` into the `X-Request-ID` response header.

steps.title: `/metrics`
steps.content_md:
Eight counters, same names in all tracks (see `GET /metrics` in `spec/openapi.yaml`):

| Counter | Incremented when |
|---|---|
| `shopflow_users_registered_total` | a registration succeeds |
| `shopflow_logins_failed_total` | a login is rejected (watch it for credential stuffing) |
| `shopflow_orders_placed_total` | a checkout creates a new order |
| `shopflow_checkout_replays_total` | a checkout was answered from its Idempotency-Key (retries, double taps) |
| `shopflow_webhooks_duplicate_total` | the payment provider redelivered an event we had already processed |
| `shopflow_orders_expired_total` | the expiry job cancelled an unpaid order (Step 7.6) |
| `shopflow_ai_fallback_total` | an AI call fell back to the offline rules/template |
| `shopflow_llm_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped an LLM call (Step 7.5) |

The replay and duplicate counters are worth a second look: in v1.0 the protections from ADR-0004 worked
silently. Now you can *see* how often they save you.

They are hand-rolled on purpose: the Prometheus text format is just
```text
# HELP shopflow_logins_failed_total Login attempts answered with 401.
# TYPE shopflow_logins_failed_total counter
shopflow_logins_failed_total 3
```
In a bigger service you would use Micrometer (Java), `prometheus-client` (Python) or `prom-client` (Node).
`/metrics` is public in this course project; in production you would restrict it to the scraper's network.

steps.title: Game day: the LLM hangs
steps.content_md:
A dead LLM is easy: the connection is refused and the fallback answers in milliseconds. A **hanging** LLM
is worse: it accepts the connection and never answers, so every search that needs it waits for the full
`LLM_TIMEOUT_MS` (5 s by default). That is what an overloaded hosted model or a stuck local Ollama looks like.
1. Start the stack at v1.0.0: `git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait`.
2. Get the script from the reference: `git show phase-7-end:scripts/game-day.sh > /tmp/game-day.sh && chmod +x /tmp/game-day.sh`,
   then `/tmp/game-day.sh <track>`. It creates a product and a customer, then runs four phases of
   10 searches each (`GET /api/v1/search/assist?q=running shoes under 3000 in stock`): **offline**
   baseline, a **healthy** fake LLM, the fake LLM **hanging**, and the LLM **back**. While the LLM hangs
   it also fires 50 searches at once and measures `/health` and `GET /cart` (the checkout path) meanwhile. The fake LLM is a 15-line Python HTTP server in a throw-away container on the Compose network
   (`MODE=ok` answers like `/v1/chat/completions`, `MODE=hang` never answers), so no model download and no API key.
3. Write down for each phase: status codes, average and maximum latency, the assist `provider` and
   `fallback` flag, the warnings in the logs, and (from v1.1) the counters. Did any search fail? Was any
   slow? Did the slow searches slow down `/health` or the cart? (In the reference run they slowed the
   Python track's `/health` to 4 s: its worker threads were all waiting for the LLM.)
4. Write `docs/postmortem-<date>-llm-hang.md`: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, what went well,
   what to improve, action items. Blameless: describe systems, not people. Read the reference
   post-mortem **after** writing yours (`git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-llm-hang.md`).

steps.title: Fix: an LLM circuit breaker
steps.content_md:
Wrap the one LLM client (shared by description drafts and search assist) in a `CircuitBreaker`:
- **CLOSED:** calls go through. 3 failures **in a row** open the circuit.
- **OPEN:** calls fail immediately (the caller uses its offline fallback) for 30 s, and
  `shopflow_llm_short_circuits_total` is incremented.
- **HALF-OPEN:** after the cooldown, exactly **one** trial call goes through. Success closes the circuit;
  failure re-opens it for another 30 s.

Test it with a fake clock and a fake client (no sleeping in tests): 3 failures → the 4th call does not reach
the client; advance the clock 30 s → one trial; a concurrent second call during the trial is short-circuited.

<!-- track:java -->
`ai/CircuitBreaker.java` implements `LlmClient`, so `AppConfig` wraps the HTTP client once and both
`LlmWriter` and `LlmParser` receive the wrapped instance. State changes are `synchronized`;
the slow HTTP call happens **outside** the lock.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `app/ai.py` has the same `chat()` signature as the HTTP client, a `threading.Lock`
around state changes and `time.monotonic` as the default clock (wall-clock time can jump).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `src/ai.ts` wraps the client's `chat()`. Node is single-threaded, but `await` still
interleaves requests, so the `trialRunning` flag matters exactly as it does in Java and Python.
<!-- /track -->

Re-run the game day on your branch: in the *hang* phase the first 3 searches still wait for the timeout,
the other 7 answer in milliseconds with `fallback: true` (average ≈ 1.5 s instead of ≈ 5 s). In the *back* phase the circuit stays open until the
30 s cooldown has passed, then one trial call closes it again.

steps.title: Maintenance change: a payment window for unpaid orders (v1.1.0)
steps.content_md:
The problem from the shop floor: checkout decrements stock immediately (ADR-0002), so a customer who
checks out and never pays locks those units **forever**. v1.1 gives every order a payment window.
1. `spec/db/migrations/V2__order_payment_window.sql`:
   `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT (now() + INTERVAL '15 minutes');`
   then backfill existing rows (`created_at + 15 minutes`) and add a **partial index**
   `ON orders (expires_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT'`. The column has a default, so v1.0.0 code
   that does not know it keeps inserting orders during a rolling deploy.
2. Checkout sets `expires_at = now + RESERVATION_TTL` (15 minutes) explicitly.
3. A new transition `PENDING_PAYMENT --expire--> CANCELLED` (restock + `order.cancelled`), and an
   admin job `POST /api/v1/admin/orders/expire` that cancels overdue orders (oldest first, at most 100
   per call) and answers `{"expired": n}`. It uses the **same compare-and-set** as every other
   transition, so an order whose payment arrives at the same moment is either PAID or expired, never
   both. A payment that arrives after the expiry is handled by the existing rule: refund requested.
4. `Order` gains `expiresAt`. Adding a field is backward compatible; removing or renaming one is not.
5. `spec/openapi.yaml` → `version: 1.1.0`; `CHANGELOG.md` → `## [1.1.0]`; bump the track's version.
6. Tests first: the expiry service tests (only overdue unpaid orders, restock, the race with a webhook),
   an API test for the admin endpoint (`403` for customers), an integration test against the real index.
7. Release: `git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "ShopFlow v1.1.0" && git push origin main --follow-tags`.
   `deploy.yml` publishes `:1.1.0` and moves `:latest`. In production a scheduler (a cron job calling
   the endpoint every minute) runs the expiry; the endpoint keeps it testable and observable.

would make it unsafe (NOT NULL without a default, volatile defaults on big tables, renames, long locks)?
How would I roll it back?

`docs/postmortem-…-llm-hang.md` with real numbers from your game day.

One merged Dependabot PR.

quiz.q: Why validate an incoming `X-Request-ID` before echoing it?
options: An unvalidated value could inject newlines or fake fields into logs and headers
quiz.explanation: Treat every header as untrusted input. A strict allow-list regex is the simplest defence.

quiz.q: During the game day every search still returned 200. Why is a hanging LLM still an incident?
options: Every search waited for the full LLM timeout, so shoppers felt 5 s of latency and server threads/connections were tied up
quiz.explanation: Graceful degradation kept correctness (the rules fallback answered) but not latency. Availability is also about how long users wait.

quiz.q: What does the circuit breaker do in the OPEN state?
options: Skips the LLM call immediately so the caller uses its offline fallback, until the cooldown ends
Switches to a different LLM provider
quiz.explanation: It turns a slow failure into a fast one. After the cooldown one half-open trial checks whether the LLM has recovered.

quiz.q: Why does `expires_at` get `NOT NULL DEFAULT (now() + INTERVAL '15 minutes')` instead of plain `NOT NULL`?
options: Postgres requires a default on every column
v1.0.0 code that does not know the column keeps inserting orders during a rolling deploy; the default fills it in
quiz.explanation: Expand first, (optionally) contract later. A `NOT NULL` column without a default would make every v1.0.0 checkout fail the moment V2 is applied.

quiz.q: Adding `expiresAt` to the order response and a new admin endpoint is a … change.
quiz.explanation: SemVer: new optional fields are minor. Removing or renaming a field would be major (2.0.0).

quiz.q: Which metric would you alert on to spot a credential-stuffing attack?
quiz.explanation: Many rejected logins in a short time is the classic signal. The fix (rate limiting per IP/account) is listed as a gap in Phase 8.

quiz.q: What makes a post-mortem "blameless"?
options: It focuses on how the system and process allowed the failure, not on who made a mistake
quiz.explanation: People hide problems when they fear blame. Blameless reviews produce better action items.

recap: Correlation IDs, MDC/context propagation and structured JSON logs without secrets.
Prometheus counters and the text exposition format.
Game days, blameless post-mortems, and why "hangs" is worse than "down".
The circuit-breaker pattern, tested with a fake clock.
Expand-style, backward-compatible migrations, a race-safe background job, and SemVer minor releases.
Dependency maintenance with Dependabot, and the role of CI as the safety net.
